scope.note: Client-to-host direction only. Host-to-client *Result types are authored by the host, so they disclose nothing the host did not already have. This file records what an untrusted host can OBSERVE; it is not an integrity model, so who may forge a field is out of scope except for the `signed` annotation.

excludedSurfaces.reason: Group chat is outside the package scope of the write-up; these entries would have no table row to map to, which would hollow out the unmapped-is-a-failure rule.

Device registration and runtime-auth state. Host-visible and real, but the write-up models the inbox and storage components; these entries would have no table row to map to, which would hollow out the unmapped-is-a-failure rule. Enumerating it is its own work.

engineAndFrontEnds.reason: The core engine, its FFI surface, and the CLI and desktop front ends. Their types are commands, events, effects and view models; whatever of theirs reaches a host does so by being one of the wire types, never by being serialized itself.

localState.reason: Client state, in memory or in the local store. Serialized to disk behind the passphrase-derived key, never to a host; Corrupt is where the write-up accounts for it.

mlsBoundary.reason: The MLS library boundary. What crosses it is RFC 9420's wire format, which the write-up assumes rather than models; the only part of it a host sees is the wrapped frame in Envelope.bytes, enumerated there.

support.reason: Signature framing, error plumbing, logging, filesystem helpers, outbound fetch, and this checker itself. Nothing here defines a type that is serialized anywhere.

nonSyntacticLeakage.note: Measured, not conceded: the corpus derives a `#len` leaf for every string a host sees, and a payload's length reports as carrying the message it wraps. The assertion is the ideal's own statement about `|m|` - content may reach the host as a length and in no other shape. Rotation is now the loudest thing on a lane. A rotation carries the rotating party's whole signed bundle rather than a reference to it — roughly four to six times an ordinary message, separable by size alone — and rotation is triggered by how many messages a party has itself sent, so the two directions of one conversation rotate on correlated schedules. Both inboxes therefore show a size-distinctive, time-correlated periodic event. This stays inside the ceiling tab:inbox already concedes (volume and timing), and it bought the counterparty callback and Definition 3; it is recorded because a repair that moves a conceded parameter should be written down, and it is the first quantity the partition test should measure rather than estimate.
Doubled by the R1 rotation change; recorded there as a traffic-pattern cost. Also directly readable today from PrivateMessage.content_type and epoch; after the R3 wrap only size class remains.

PrivateMessage.group_id, epoch and content_type are cleartext in every frame and identical at both inboxes, which is why the lane wrap exists. Measured now rather than argued: the corpus parses a frame header out of any payload it can, at each offset a frame can begin at, and finds none - while making the wrap a pass-through puts the conversation id at both inboxes and fails the assertion. The first attempt at this probe was silent because direct_frame prefixes a tag byte, which hid the header without the wrap doing any work; the offsets close that.
Records are deleted only at retention expiry, not on ack, so the host holds every envelope header for 30 days past delivery.
Already carried by the Linkability row as `sender address`. The network layer is not addressable here, so application-layer anonymity is the ceiling of any repair in this component.

limits: Containment is not information, and on the TypeScript side that is still the only question asked: the key checks look for a sentinel SUBSTRING, so a key that was a hash or a bucket of a secret would pass clean. It is tolerable there because the key builders are pure functions of their arguments and the test renders them on known inputs. On the Rust side the limit is gone: src/leakage_corpus.rs measures `carries` by varying real secrets across real engine runs and comparing partitions, which catches a hash exactly as it catches the cleartext. The hash is not hypothetical — a SHA-256 of the sender's user id inserted as a header was reported as carrying that identity, and the substring check is provably silent on it.
Non-syntactic channels are not modelled at all; see nonSyntacticLeakage, where checked:false records that their absence is a decision and not an oversight.

`fate` uses the Fate column's vocabulary, but nothing here checks that the write-up actually assigns that fate. CI proves a human recorded a decision in a coordinate system the write-up cannot silently rename, not that the two agree. That reconciliation is still by hand, and it is deliberately the only coupling: a generator that rendered these entries into a table the write-up did not read was deleted rather than repaired.

Inhabitation (bits) is measured asymmetrically, because that is all a finite script can support. `constant` and `absent` are refutable and are refuted: one varying observation in the corpus fails the row. `inhabited` is not established by the corpus, because a value this script holds still - a sequence number, the single runtime id both parties share here - moves in a longer execution, and declaring it constant would be a false claim about the protocol. So an `inhabited` row the corpus never sees vary is corroborated where it can be and left standing otherwise.

Compile-time exhaustiveness has holes: serde(flatten), a serde_json::Value-typed field, serde(untagged), or a non-exhaustive match elsewhere would each make these checks go quiet rather than red. None are present in the in-scope types today.

Widening `carries` to silence a red is still a one-line edit to this file, but it no longer helps: host_view_is_a_function_of_l compares the measured set to the declared one by EQUALITY in both directions, so a row that claims more than the corpus observes fails exactly as loudly as one that claims less.

lane and mid are not sentinels and do not need to be: the claim worth testing about a lane is that the two inboxes of one conversation share no token, and host_view_shares_no_token_across_inboxes states exactly that over a corpus with both sides in it. Collapsing new_lane_pair to one value, or removing the lane wrap so the MLS frame header is readable, each makes it red.

The group-outbox spill keys are assembled inline at services/cloudflare/src/group-outbox/service.ts, not through leakage-keys.ts, so the TS check that every minted template is recorded here cannot see them. This is the same failure the module partition on the Rust side closed, one level down: a key built at a call site is invisible to a check that reads the builders. Not repaired in this round, because repairing it means deciding whether the group-outbox surface enters the enumeration at all, and scope.excludedSurfaces currently says it does not.

welcome-pickup is the one object named by a digest rather than by a fresh random: it is pure R2 with no Durable Object beside it, so the name has to be one both sides recompute from the capability the fetcher presents. The builder therefore does not itself guarantee the name carries nothing — the caller does, by passing a hash.

The corpus varies six inputs: each party's identity, each party's message text, the attachment's name and its length. A field determined by an input held fixed measures as constant, and a field determined by one generated per execution measures as fresh. The device key is the case that matters: it is minted at enrolment, not supplied, so no matrix separates it, and `recipient_device` accordingly left the carries vocabulary on the Rust surfaces. In the modelled scope of one device per party it adds nothing to `recipient_user`, and within a single execution the cross-inbox assertion covers it.

The corpus's recorder plays the host, and every value it writes on the host's behalf - a sequence number, an object name, a first-contact request id - is minted the way the real host mints it and never derived from what the client sent. This is the one hand-maintained edge in the mechanism. Deriving a blob name from the client's task id, for instance, would manufacture a conversation identifier into storageRef.ref, and the red would be the recorder's fault rather than the protocol's.

Relocation is not in the corpus. Its host-visible delta is an endpoint origin, which belongs to L_net and is already accepted there; the signed bundle and the new inbound lane it announces ride inside the wrap, where the host sees only a payload length.

Inbox bookkeeping: the record head, the ack watermark, the retention and limit settings, and the append counter the inbox answers every append with. That counter runs over every append whatever becomes of the record, so the number discloses nothing about whether the record was admitted or queued; it is also the closer analogue of the i the ideal returns, which counts every send rather than the ones an adversary chose to deliver.

The admission credential, and the quota partition. A 1:1 payload is placed in the recipient runtime, which admits the sender on the same lane it admits its envelopes on; revoking the contact deletes one key and stops both.

A fresh 256-bit name. Read access was always gated on an independent capability, so the identifiers this key used to carry bought nothing and cost a cross-inbox token: the same key reached the recipient inbox as envelope.storageRef.ref, and its conversation segment was identical at both ends.

protectedFields.note: app:{conversation_id}:{nonce}:{sender_device_id}. Nothing in the host view carries it; the earlier claim that the header duplicated it was left over from a header that no longer exists.
Random 128-bit local MLS group_id; no longer duplicated on the 1:1 envelope header.

The 1:1 envelope header has not named the sender since the header shrank to four fields. Until the object key became opaque this still reached the host through envelope.storageRef.ref, which is why it was recorded as duplicated rather than confidential — a claim about a header that no longer held it.
Same as sender_user_id, and transitively worse: a device id names its user.
Transitively: the header carries recipient_device_id, and a device id is format!("device:{user_fp}:{device_fp}"), so it already names the user.
Fan-out width is deliberately hidden; the header names one recipient device.

group.reason: Group chat is outside the package scope of the write-up.

hostToClient.reason: Authored by the host; discloses nothing it did not have.

deferred.reason: The identity-publication and runtime-auth surface. Real and host-visible, but a distinct surface that R3 does not touch; enumerating it is its own piece of work. Listed here so a NEW type still fails the partition guard.

localOnly.reason: Never serialized to a host. ProtectedAppMessage is covered separately by protectedFields, and AuthenticatedDirectCommit is what survives verifying a rival commit's detached signature — an epoch and a hash, with no name left in it.
